newsitem.title: INDIA: India's RBI seen boosting credit,firm on inflation.
newsitem.headline: India's RBI seen boosting credit,firm on inflation.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will seek a balance between loosening credit while keeping monetary growth in check when it presents a half-yearly strategy paper next week, analysts said on Tuesday.

The central bank, while it enjoys independence from India's government, must strike a policy that provides a monetary environment to match Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's growth, investment and business-friendly budget.
The central bank will unveil its monetary and credit policy for the first half of the 1997/98 (April-March) financial year on April 15.
But the RBI is receiving scant attention in the tense days ahead of a crucial confidence vote for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority government on Friday.
The country's Congress party triggered a political crisis on March 30 when it withdrew vital support for Deve Gowda's ruling coalition.

Unlike Chidambaram's ambitious budget -- which must still be passed by parliament and remains hostage to the fate of the government -- the RBI is expected to map out a low key strategy and maintain a check on inflation, analysts said.
"The prime task will be containing inflationary pressures," said Aashish Pitale, analyst at ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec), the Indian affiliate of U.S. investment bank J.P. Morgan.
Inflation, as measured by the wholesale price index, was 7.51 percent year-on-year for the week ended March 22. It was 5.01 percent in the same period last year.

"Inflation is higher than the RBI's target of around six percent while M3 growth at around 16 percent year-on-year is in line with their target," said Anindya Chatterjee, economist at NatWest Markets.
"So I do not think any loosening in monetary policy is warranted," Chatterjee said.
That has to be reconciled with a need to stimulate credit growth and satisfy companies calling out for lower lending rates, the analysts said.

State-run banks' lowest prime lending rates are currently 14 percent, and gilt prices leapt last week on expectations that the central bank will announce measures which will lead to a fall in interest rates.
The most likely step will be a cut in banks' deposit rates, which the RBI has set at 10 percent for deposits of 30 days to one year, the analysts said.
"The RBI will have to look at ways to boost credit growth," said I-sec's Pitale.
Credit has grown by 153.13 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) so far in 1996/97 against deposit growth of 554.35 billion rupees in the same period.
This is in sharp contrast to the previous year when credit grew by 17.2 percent or 364.73 billion rupees against deposit growth of only 308.6 billion or 8.0 percent.
"What is needed is to keep the post-February 28 sentiment alive," Sunil Bhandare, economic advisor to the Tata group of companies, India's largest industrial combine, said.
Bhandare was referring to the day Chidambaram unveiled proposals slashing personal and corporate taxes and excise duties.
The subsequent bull run in Indian equity markets added more than 15 percent to the Bombay Stock Exchange's (BSE) top 30 index, which peaked on March 3 at 4007.91.
But the Congress party's shock decision to withdraw support for the United Front coalition 10 days ago erased all the gains.
On Monday the BSE index closed at 3520.49, a little over one percent higher than pre-budget levels.
Bhandare said heavy government borrowing requirements in fiscal 1997/98 posed potential problems for corporate borrowers.
But RBI governor C.Rangarajan has said the M3 monetary growth target provided enough room to satisfy government needs without squeezing corporates out of the market.
The 1997/98 budget proposals show net government borrowings to be 33 percent higher from 1996/97 levels at 338.20 billion rupees.
($ = 35.86 rupees)
